lessonRef.unitTitle: Quantitative Reasoning, Units, and Rational Exponents
lessonRef.focus: radical and rational-exponent notation and rewriting
lessonRef.title: Performance task planning: radical and rational-exponent notation and rewriting

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: This example shows how to justify a modelling choice.

steps: Subtracting the rational number 5 would leave √3 rational, but √3 is irrational.
The assumption fails, so 5 + √3 is irrational.

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Decide what the quantities are before you compute anything.

items.prompt: Option A delivers 36 units of output over 6 hours. Option B delivers 72 units over 8 hours. Which has the greater output per hour?
choices: There is not enough information without knowing the total hours available.

items.prompt: A rectangular plot measures 76.5 m by 7.1 m, each measured to the nearest tenth of a metre. Report the area to 1 decimal place.
You are building a model of the rate at which a reservoir is draining. Which unit should the modelled quantity be reported in?

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: Plan in writing: what you will model, why that model, and how you will check it.

items.prompt: A delivery drone operates at 51 kilometers per hour. Express this rate in meters per minute.
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: Rewrite the index-3 radical expression 3√(x^6) using a rational exponent, in lowest terms.
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
